\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:ml-family}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my father, mother, and my older and younger brothers and sisters in Malayalam.}

Say the six family words in age-graded pairs, and note that Malayalam built its own sibling set rather than tracking Tamil's.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{അച്ഛൻ} \ml{അമ്മ} \ml{ചേട്ടൻ} \ml{അനിയൻ} \ml{ചേച്ചി} \ml{അനിയത്തി}]{\ml{അച്ഛൻ}, \ml{അമ്മ}, and four sibling words — Malayalam's own set}

\label{lesson:ML-C12-kudumbam}



\begin{quote}
Malayalam and Tamil share a great deal of their vocabulary — but family words are where Malayalam goes its own way further than you might expect, while still keeping the family's signature age-first sibling system.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{അച്ഛൻ}} (\emph{acchan}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{father}\textquotedblright{} — a different form from Tamil's \emph{appā}; \textbf{this word's own deeper origin is less settled} than the simple \emph{appā/amma} pattern, and worth a linguist's extra look.
  \item \textbf{\ml{അമ്മ}} (\emph{amma}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mother}\textquotedblright{} — matches the family's shared \emph{amma} pattern closely.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Malayalam} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ചേട്ടൻ}} (\emph{cēṭṭan}) & \textbf{older} brother \\
\textbf{\ml{അനിയൻ}} (\emph{aniyan}) & \textbf{younger} brother \\
\textbf{\ml{ചേച്ചി}} (\emph{cēcci}) & \textbf{older} sister \\
\textbf{\ml{അനിയത്തി}} (\emph{aniyatti}) & \textbf{younger} sister \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Notice these don't closely match Tamil/Kannada/Telugu's \emph{aṇṇaṉ/anna}, \emph{tambi/tammuḍu}, \emph{akkā/akka}, or \emph{tangai/celli} — Malayalam built its own set of sibling words. But the \textbf{structure} is identical: \textbf{four} words, not two, split by whether the sibling is \textbf{older or younger than you} — the same signature pattern you've now seen across all four Dravidian languages, even where the specific words diverge.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}acchan, amma\textquotedblright{} — father, mother
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cēṭṭan, aniyan\textquotedblright{} — older/younger brother
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cēcci, aniyatti\textquotedblright{} — older/younger sister
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do Malayalam's sibling words closely match Tamil's? (\textbf{No} — Malayalam built its own distinct set (cēṭṭan, aniyan, cēcci, and aniyatti), unlike how closely Kannada and Telugu track Tamil.) Does Malayalam still split siblings by age? (\textbf{Yes} — four words, older vs. younger, the same structural pattern across the whole Dravidian family.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\ml{◌ു} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S07-vowel-sign-u}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ൾ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌ു}}
\textbf{\ml{◌ു}} — \emph{u}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{u}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{◌ു} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{സുഖമാണോ}?} — how are you? (lit. \textquotedblleft{}are you well?\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{സുഖം}} \emph{sukhaṁ} — well-being — and the reply "\ml{സുഖമാണ്}
  \item \textbf{\ml{താമസിക്കുക}} \emph{tāmasikkuka} — to live, to stay
  \item \textbf{\ml{ജോലി} \ml{ചെയ്യുക}} \emph{jōli ceyyuka} — to work (lit. \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{◌ു} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{◌ു} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{◌ു} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{സുഖമാണോ}?  ·  \ml{സുഖം}  ·  \ml{നമസ്കാരം}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{◌ു} three times, saying \emph{u} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{◌ു} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{◌ു}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{u} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ña]{\ml{ഞ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S115-letter-nya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{മ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ഞ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഞ}} — \emph{ña}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ñ}, it is \textbf{ña}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{ഞ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} — I
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{സംസാരിക്കുന്നു}} — I speak Malayalam
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്} \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മൂന്ന്} \ml{നാല്} \ml{അഞ്ച്}} — one to five
  \item \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കൾ} \ml{ചൊവ്വ} \ml{ബുധൻ} \ml{വ്യാഴം} \ml{വെള്ളി} \ml{ശനി} \ml{ഞായർ}} — the seven weekdays
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{ഞ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{ഞ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{ഞ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{ഞാൻ}  ·  \ml{നമസ്കാരം}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{ഞ} three times, saying \emph{ña} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{ഞ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{ഞ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ña}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
